Journalism can be a hard topic to cover in film without adding a bunch of unnecessary drama to make it interesting. But Spotlight has the benefit of a great script with very natural dialogue. Nothing here feels forced of feigned. It immersively chronicles the Boston Globe's long-time investigation into the Catholic Church sex-abuse scandal.

As a guy who grew up in the Catholic Church, it isn't easy watching this film and knowing that it's the Catholic Church who is to blame. But like any place where you have people in a position of power, you're going to have those who abuse that power. The Church is no different. And just like not every cop is racist and not every black person plays basketball, not every priest is a child molester. Although I was an alter server as a child and luckily never experienced or heard of anyone personally who suffered through this tragedy, I do shake my head at those who tried to cover it up. 

Although the sex-abuse issues were nationwide, the film focuses mostly on the staggering numbers in the Boston Archdiocese. Catholicism in Boston has been known to be more of a culture in that city than most other places in the country. Their dependence and wholehearted belief in the Church made for a much easier target for predators. It's one thing to idolize God and hold true to your religious beliefs, but it's another to idolize other human beings. To idolize is to believe that one is not capable of fault. Well, the people of Boston held true, more than anyone, that these priests were godlike figures who could do no wrong. It was a sentiment that exuded from everywhere in that city. In California, where I live, I've never experienced anything quite like that in the 26 years I've spent as a practicing member of the Catholic faith. Not to say that these priests aren't expected to lead a holier life than most of our own, but then we look back to that whole abuse of power thing. 

As for the movie, it's very well done. The acting is superb. Director, Tom McCarthy, gets the very best performance out of each of his actors. Especially Liev Schreiber, who does his best Steven Wright impression, always remaining soft spoken, yet intimidating. He never overplays his character, which isn't necessarily easy for an actor to do. 

Mark Ruffalo is perhaps the biggest standout. He's an absolute phenomenon here. He commits so much to every one of his character's idiosyncrasies that it's truly hypnotizing. 

The script is also great, doing well to explain and give background on a lot of the more convoluted details of the story. It can, however, be hard to follow all the names that are being spewed at you, remembering who everyone is. The story moves along briskly with only a slight thinning out for about 10 minutes towards the end.

But the one thing that Spotlight does pretty poorly at is depth, almost as if it's deliberately trying not to have any. It's anything but a character study. There's a lot of implied background for the characters, but you can't help but want a little more. Even in the macro sense, it has several perfect opportunities to explore the psychology behind these child molesters, but the film never really takes advantage of them, thus leaving a few scenes feeling unnecessary.

Despite making unbiased claims, the film does have a bit of an agenda of its own. It tells of certain characters' stated struggles with their faith, although they had already admitted to being lapsed. While it never shows how the Church's scandal would affect actual churchgoers.

Although I'm not commending any of it, I know why Cardinal Law chose to cover up all of those scandals. When you have a society that is full of ignorant people who constantly generalize everything, then you are going to have other people who try and cover up these instances in fear that the general public will, indeed, generalize. And so it happened anyway. Those who aren't Catholic go into this movie and may look at the Church in a negative light. But like I said, people love to think in absolutes. I, myself, don't idolize anyone, but can totally recognize that these are definitely horrible tragedies to be ashamed of.

It's tough for me to say exactly why Spotlight worked for me.  There's nothing spectacular that really stands out about it, and in many other films that tried the same style I'd call it boring and pedestrian.  Somehow though, Spotlight pulls it off.  It's plays things simple, and maybe that's what makes it work.  It's the subtlety of it all that makes the whole thing work.  The facts are big, but reactions are subtle, and that makes it all feel more genuine.
I don't think there's anything very special about Spotlight's directing (which makes this year's Oscar nominations pretty surprising), but what really makes the movie work are the performances and the script.    I recognized a lot of the actors at first, but pretty quickly forgot about their past roles and just saw them as people.  They discover horrific details about the catholic sex abuse scandal, but each new reveal doesn't lead them to some huge Oscar-bait outburst, but a more genuine response.  Oftentimes they are simply speechless, and that feels very real.  The script is also great.  It drops you right in the middle of things, these events have already been happening for a while, but it doesn't take long to catch up and it respects you enough to expect that you can.  There was never any point when I was really bored by the movie.
If I have an outright criticism of the movie it's that I maybe would have liked more information, but I don't think that's this movies job.  It tells a very specific perspective of the events unfolding, it would just be nice if there were other movies that gave more perspective.  As this singular perspective though, it works really well.  There's not a lot of character development or anything like that, it's really just the investigation, but that's more than enough to carry the film.  If watching news reporters investigate a story isn't your thing, I get it, it's not going to be riveting for everyone, but it was for me.  I can't really pinpoint the magic ingredient that made Spotlight work so well, but damnit all it really did work so damn well.

"Spotlight" is about the team of investigative reporters of the Boston Globe that goes by the same name who uncovered the child molestation and cover up scandal by the clergy of the local Catholic Archdiocese. The reporting won the team the 2003 Pulitzer Prize.

"Spotlight" is an ode to investigative reporting that focuses on accuracy, fact checking and restraint in publishing a story until all the facts and circumstances have been fully covered. It is a discipline and an art form that is almost lost in today's world of journalism where the focus have been subverted to get higher ratings (TV), keep subscribers and maintain readership (print media) or to please advertisers (both).

The film features a superb cast that includes Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Liev Schreiber, John Slattery and Stanley Tucci, to name a few. The ensemble acting is magnificent. As to the story, it is told with meticulous attention to detail.

"Spotlight" reminds us of "All The President's Men", the 1976 film that focused on the Watergate scandal. But more importantly, this film shows what true and hard-working journalists can accomplish when the focus is on the victims - even if it means taking on an institution that has power, money and resources. It is about performing due diligence and telling an accurate story that, in the end, looks at a system that allowed a cover up to happen.

VIEWS ON FILM review by Jesse Burleson

"I wanna keep digging" quips the character of Walter Robinson (Michael Keaton), a well respected reporter at Beantown's most heralded newspaper. What can I say, I "dug" all 128 minutes of the vehicle I'm about to review.

Anyway, for all Academy Award purposes and historical insight, Spotlight is the quintessential best picture nominee. It's secure, by the book filmmaking and that doesn't hurt it in any way. 1976 had All the President's Men, 1981 had Absence of Malice, 2007 had Zodiac, and now 2015 brings us "Light". All these films have one thing in common. They are dialogue-driven, feed off paranoia, and resound in crowded newsrooms. "Nose goes" gets a nose for the news. Natch!

Taking place in the early 2000's and helmed by director Tom McCarthy, Spotlight moves along like a jack rabbit. Yeah this flick is talky but it never comes off as insipid. There are a lot of continuity cuts between scenes, ensemble acting (where everyone helps each other out) of the highest order, and crackling intrigue inhabiting every frame. Alongside his previous endeavor Birdman, "Light's" lead in Michael Keaton, is now two for two. His co-star (Mark Ruffalo) who got nominated for a supporting role via 2014's Foxcatcher, is also batting 1.000.

So yeah there might be a repetition in Spotlight involving every (news reporter) caricature interrogating a victim and/or a suspect. No matter. This Open Road Films release rings true because Josh Singer's screenplay is tight and engrossing. What we have amongst the muck, is the best movie of the year (so far). And just like one of my other top picks (2015's Black Mass), the city of Boston swallows the proceedings whole as if Michael Phelps decided to inhale tons of hot dogs. You want to see actual events depicted that involve a massive cover-up among the Roman Catholic priests? You'll get that in "Light". You want the 9/11 attacks to be used effectively as a backdrop? You'll get that as well. You wanna witness a small investigative team unravel the secrets behind so many young churchgoers getting molested? It's all there. And do you want to revel in having the Boston Globe be the locale where all the news shtick goes down? Prego. Finally, do you want a cast that includes Liev Schreiber, Stanley Tucci, Rachel McAdams, and Billy Crudup? Who wouldn't.

All in all, Spotlight involves behind-the-scenes preoccupation in small rooms and quiet, open spaces. Every nuance between the troupers sticks. With its disciplined magnetism and critical darling demur, "Light" shines brightly. Rating: 4 stars.

Was upon viewing, and may still be at the end of this great movie year, my favorite -- an old-fashioned kind of telling of an old-fashioned industry, newspapering, fueled by old-fashioned virtue, e.g., honor, honesty, truth. It's remarkable that a story centered upon almost unspeakable crimes -- the sexual abuse of thousands of young boys (and some girls too) by members of the Roman Catholic clergy -- is really a mystery story about finding the proof that will expose the monsters in the church hierarchy who knew about the crimes, covered them up, then lied about the coverup. Virtually everyone in the story in Catholic Boston knows each other and is steeped in the culture that made such venality possible for so long -- the priests, the church administration, its influential supporters, the cops, the prosecutors, and indeed, the leadership of the Boston Globe. Except for two outsiders, an Armenian-American defense attorney and a Jewish editor who pushed the investigative unit, known as Spotlight, to dig, and then dig harder, at immense personal  costs to the members of the team. Like the films of Frank Capra, Spotlight brings the story to a rousing finale -- you want to stand up and cheer, were it not for the horror that remains at the center of the story, to this day.

"How do you say no to God? This isn't just physical abuse; it's spiritual abuse." Surprisingly, the headline-grabbing Catholic Church sex scandal is not even the real focus of this powerhouse display of acting and directing. Yes, the abuses are horrendous, even when they are just being spoken and not shown. However, the true star of Spotlight is an intense and loving look at the nearly-lost art of the journalistic process. McCarthy directs with a refreshing lack of glamour or melodrama, leaving us with this question: if our "heroes" succeed here, who really wins?

Yet another astounding piece of cinema making its way to us just as the year comes to a close. Spotlight is the slow burning but riveting tale of the monolithic Boston Globe, based on a true story, when a small team within the paper, called Spotlight, are forced to drop their current investigation and their laid back attitude, in favor of a more audacious and high pressured investigation into molestation in the catholic church, they soon find that not only are their fears true, but uncover a plethora of cases and resistance from the church itself. Spotlight could easily be a David Fincher moment, brimming with brilliant character pieces, rooted in american style and oozing intrigue from the work go, and Tom McCarthy even borrows from Fincher's, Zodiac, in one or more shots. However McCarthy decides to fight back the darkness, somewhat, and leave us with a daunting but uplifting piece, that by the end will completely envelop you. Its a slow burning affair, with not a lot going on, subdued performances, with the exception of Ruffalo and nothing to flashy in the visual department, McCarthy is clearly letting the story and his script do all the heavy lifting and for the briefest of moments the film does feel a little lost to begin with. By the time the 2nd act comes around, not only have we lost ourselves in a weighty investigation, but there is a fare share of excellent drama and performance to go about. The cast are all terrific, everyone from Keaton, Schrieber, Crudup, McAdams, Tucci and Slattery all do some solid work, grounding the lifeblood of the Globe and making the piece feel extremely human and unlike an Oscar nomination, however its Mark Ruffalo's completely riveting and game changing performance that turns this cast and indeed film from a good time, into a great time. He just becomes a character, even with his, huge stature as the Hulk, Ruffalo is fearless and capable of completely bypassing any connection with his CGI counterpart, by just deeply rooting himself in good old fashioned performance, from mannerisms to accent, really lending a sense of realism to the whole affair. Its a great picture all around, and thats Spotlights biggest flaw, if you can call it that, it appears to play it safe. The film takes quite a bit of time to start leaving you a little more time than you want, to begin to pick apart the film itself, by the end you will really love the final product but will not be able to shake the feeling that McCarthy may have played this one, just a little too safe. Its understandable given the content but in this case the careful approach can be felt by the final frame. It's a solid effort, a film more subdued and down scaled than a lot of others on offer this year, strongly recommend.

In Spotlight directed by Tom McCarthy journalist is questioned on his core. In 2001 The Boston Globe hires a new editor Marty Baron (Liev Schreiber) with the promise of searching for better stories and more solid journalism work. Walter Robinson (Michael Keaton) is the head of "Spotlight" team a group of journalist of the Globe whose articles are investigative nature, but can take up to a year to publish. The film start with an incident of a priest who is be taking a police precinct in Boston for allegedly molesting a kid from the parish in the 70's the case seems to go under the table when the archdioceses gets involved to solve the problem. Tom McCarthy set the foundation of the story by proving that this is lawless crimes that can be hide so easily in front of the police. Back to 2001 Baron reads a small article that talks about a pedophile priest John Geoghan and how the archbishop of Boston knew about it and  did nothing to stop it. The spotlight team is been asked to start an investigation about the peophile cases in the church of Boston.

The spotlight team start to work Michael Resends (Mark Ruffalo) Sacha Pfeiffer (Rachel McAdams) and Matt Carroll (Brian d'Arcy James) with a lot of skepticism but quickly revealing shocking information about the victims, their abusers, and how the elite was forced to hide the truth to keep an image of a perfect clerical society in Boston. 

The film is powerful with strong performances by all the cast, Thomas Newman deliver a compelling original score, Tom McArdle gives the film the perfect pace on a outstanding editing.

Spotlight is not about journalist who becomes heroes, is about the power of ethics and the search for the truth, it's also about mistakes made and when you search for that truth you have to risk so many things in your life.

SPOTLIGHT is an undeniably powerful film, one whose subject matter is absolutely infuriating and disheartening, though if I'm being honest, it kind of coasts on that, and on the strength of the acting on display.  The filmmaking is very solid and workmanlike, but nowhere near the kind of bravura effort some in the critical community have argued it is; to me, it feels like an HBO movie, and you can take that any way you want.  Now, one could certainly make the case that to turn this story into some kind of flashy cinematic showcase would have been absolutely tone-deaf, and on a certain level I agree.  Yet, I still think the movie as a whole is a bit too restrained, a bit too low-key; I was captivated by the material, not so much by the cinema of it all.  The strongest element of the movie (unquestionably, in my mind) is the screenplay, which handles an insane amount of information, dates, names, and locations with apparent total ease, and it presents this information in ways that do not allow the facts to become jumbled up in the minds of the audience.  Just below the screenplay in importance are the cast members, each of whom do exemplary work, to a person being grounded and real.  Some might jump to Keaton or Ruffalo as the standouts, but Schreiber could be the movie's quiet MVP.  It's hard not to bring your own baggage to this story, and as a Catholic, it brought back all those things I felt when the actual story broke; the film is a powerful reminder... and also one I have no great desire to revisit.

Yes, it's a lot to deal with.  So this is about a specialty team of journalists that work for the Boston Globe in 2001.  When they decide to run an exposé piece about the high number of reports of child abuse within the Catholic Church, the entire system is in for a big shake-up.  Now being that I am in my Oscar crunch, I have a very high intake of films and not a lot of time to sit down and crank out these reviews (also, downtime at my day job has all but disappeared entirely, thus making this a twofold problem).  I actually watched this film over a month ago, but I can tell you one thing: it has stayed with me wholly and completely, which isn't something that I can say for a lot of other films I have taken in.  I will say that I felt like this took a good 15 - 20 minutes to get going, which is fine, as you are just getting a non-glamorous introduction to these characters before they get into the full swing of their investigation.  Once it does get going, it holds on to your attention without letting go.  It's such a tremendous ensemble performance from this all-star cast, and you really get a sense of what it is that all of these people do for a living; even if they weren't working on a piece of such high importance, their demeanor wouldn't change all that much because this is people just doing their jobs and trying to do what is right, and the film as a whole never loses grasp of that feeling.  Even the no-name actors that you haven't seen before give complementing gut-wrenching performances, and Spotlight makes you feel like a journalist, sparking your interest in the process of it all.  I have to give a very high commendation to Spotlight because where most films like this would go for the jugular at a moment's notice given the topic at hand, director Tom McCarthy approaches this with a tremendous amount of subtlety, which is something that is becoming increasingly rare to find in film these days.  Spotlight is an excellently made film that is quite hard to watch, given the despicable nature of the subject matter.  This year, I've now seen movies about child abuse and animal abuse, and it will never be something that is an easy thing to get through, so I honestly don't know how much repeat viewing one can get out of this.  For the story it tells, you experience the full spectrum of emotions; you get excited as a promising lead turns into something more, you get upset when you learn about a grown man's previous experience with a priest, and you get downright angry when you see the church trying to sweep this under the proverbial carpet.  I promise you, when you reach the end of this and you get to see a giant wall of text of affected cities, you will have an involuntary reaction in the pit of your stomach.  It's a very good thing that this movie exists, and it is utmost effective at telling a story that needed to be told.

Review: Spotlight
This seems to be a Winter movie season full of topical films with tough subject matter. Movies like Room, Concussion and The Danish Girl are already making waves. So is Spotlight, director Tom McCarthy's (The Station Agent, The Visitor) account of the Boston Globe journalism team that took on the Catholic Church and helped uncover decades of child abuse at the hands of priests. Understandably, Spotlight is one of hardest movies to watch this year simply because the subject is so unsettling. Hearing detailed accounts of child abuse isn't supposed to be easy to hear, and while the film thankfully doesn't spend enormous amounts of time wallowing in those details, it doesn't pull its punches either. McCarthy and co-writer Josh Singer deserve a lot of credit for writing what I believe is the best script of the year. It's a talkative movie, for sure, but the dialogue doesn't feel phony or unnatural, and wise decisions were made in choosing exactly what details to include to help create a motion picture that would be informative but also intriguing and well-paced.
Of course, a good script is useless without a talented cast and this one sure is a line-up: Michael Keaton, Mark Ruffalo, Rachel McAdams, Brian d'Arcy James, Liev Schreiber, John Slattery, Stanley Tucci and Billy Crudup round out an amazing cast supported by a who's-who of veteran character actors, not to mention an uncredited voice performance by Richard Jenkins. This cast shines, and even though the nominations haven't even been announced yet, it's difficult seeing any other movie taking home SAG's Outstanding Performance by a Cast in a Motion Picture award. The reason I'm making this prediction is because this is a rare film where every actor is so essential to the movie's success. Nobody feels tacked on. Nobody feels like a cameo. I also don't pity SAG nor the Academy because picking who from this cast deserves nominations is not going to be easy. Attention seems to be focused on Michael Keaton as far as awards buzz is concerned, and that's fine. He has rarely been better. If I was able to pick, however, I might shine that Oscar light on Mark Ruffalo or Brian d'Arcy James if only because their characters seem more emotionally invested in the investigation than the others and this gives both actors lots of chances to shine. Spotlight really is a master class in acting and it can't be denied that these actors have raised an already great script to an even higher level.
As I already mentioned, the film is well-paced. At just over two hours of talking and talking and talking, some movies may have become boring or repetitive, but Spotlight avoids this pitfall. Editor Tom McArdle has trimmed whatever fat there may have been well and I really can't pick out any scenes that I would have left out.
I have always loved movies about journalism. There usually seems to be a real sense of urgency to them and they usually bring out the best from their casts. Spotlight excels in its genre. I've said many times that my favorite thing to see on screen is great actors performing great scripts-but add to that a movie that is really about something important-you just can't beat that. Spotlight may not have been on everyone's list, but it should be. This one is a major contender for best of the year. 9/10?

Spotlight is the true story of an investigative branch of the Boston Globe who unearthed a massive cover-up among the Catholic Church and the astonishing number of child-molesting priests that were never brought to justice back in 2002 and with intense acting and riveting storytelling, it may be the best film based on journalism of all time. Directed by actor/writer Tom McCarthy with gusto, he certainly made a bold move taking on this project that paints what many go to for guidance in a really ugly light and you cringe more and more as you learn just how many priests were involved in this scandal. The Spotlight team is made up of character actor Brian d'Arcy James, and big-hitters: Rachel McAdams, Michael Keaton, and Mark Ruffalo in one of his strongest performances to date remaining subdued and believable with a boiling intensity in his vendetta for justice. The other supporting players are just as great with an unrecognizable Liev Schreiber, Mad Men's John Slattery, Stanley Tucci, and many others, rounding out a terrific ensemble cast that is more quality than quantity. If journalism interests you, this is your home run right here because it is not a flashy film at all and takes its time with the characters researching, interviewing, and writing this case for their paper and it's a great indication of how journalism can do some good as well! The film also plays fair and while it chastises the Church for burying it's secrets, it also shows that the reporters aren't perfect either and have made a few mistakes of their own, it would've been too easy to make this a witch-hunt film, but they thankfully don't go that route. This is a tense, realistic, and brainy drama about getting the facts straight and taking on one of the biggest cover-ups in history and it is immensely satisfying by the end and it's re-assuring to see the media in a positive light for a change.

Powerful, yet restrained, effective, thought-provoking and tense, Spotlight is a flawless example of what a perfect drama & thriller should be. A wonderful depiction of what investigative journalism is and how to make this right into a movie, Tom McCarthy's gem is a already and instant classic that easily could be considered as one of the biggest favorites at this year's Oscars. 

Based on the true story of how the so called "Spotlight" team of The Boston Globe investigated and uncovered the decade-long continuous sexual abuse in the Catholic Church in Boston, the movie impresses with its overall approach towards the story and the facts. Just like the team of journalist which handled the topic, director Tom McCarthy makes sure that the movie does the same. Restrained, focused, slow, but steadily developed, the story builds up the tension and the thrills to a sky-high level even without a single act of violence. It is a journalist drama that simply depicts how a true investigative journalism should be conducted and everyone who is or feels himself connected to the world of media, communications and journalism will be completely delighted with this movie. Another achievement of director Tom McCarthy is the fact that even though this is a journalist drama, there is enough attention paid to the victims. The multiple victims are not dehumanized as persons of journalistic interest, but do share their stories in a way that nobody, even a devoted, skeptic catholic, could remain untouched. 

In addition to the incredible way of handling the story, the cast ensemble of Spotlight is what also turns this movie into a classic. Michael Keaton, Marc Ruffalo, Rachel McAdams, Live Schreiber and the rest, are amazing. Without depicting their characters as "investigative" heroes, all of them are just professionals and human beings. They are people who are devoted to their jobs, who make mistakes, who have their concerns, worries and doubts. Special attention should be paid to the trio Keaton- Ruffalo - Schreiber. Michael Keaton has a commanding presence and absorbs the indirect tension which different institutions tried to put on his team. Marc Ruffalo's determination, energy and stubbornness won him an Oscar nomination for Best Male Supporting Act and even if he does not win it (if we consider Syvlester Stallone the favorite in the category), his performance will remain unforgettable. Last, but not least, some of the viewers (like myself) might be delighted by the performance and depiction of the executive editor Martin Baron (Liev Schreiber). Schreiber's character has the presence, behavior and charisma of what the perfect executive editor should be. 

In conclusion, Spotlight is definitely one of the top movies of 2015. A must see journalist drama, it will make you further explore this topic on the internet long after you see the final credits. With 6 Oscar nominations, currently it is almost a safe bet that this is the movie that could challenge the expected domination of The Revenant.

'Spotlight' and 'The Big Short' will forever be linked, which speaks to their quality - both based on true stories that effected lots of people, both great dramas, both Oscar-nominated films out within weeks of each other. 'Spotlight' has some laughs, but not as many as 'The Big Short', mostly due to the dark nature of the material - the uncovering of Catholic priests molesting and raping young children, for over four decades. 

The Boston Globe investigative journalism team ("Spotlight") - from when newspapers were still relevant, in 2001 - consisting of Mike (Ruffalo), Sacha (McAdams), Matt (d'Arcy James) and their editor, Robby (Keaton) are tasked with finding out if an accused priest is in fact guilty of child molestation. This comes about when their bosses, Marty (Schreiber, still looking like Sabretooth) - new at the newspaper - & Ben (Slattery) try to shake things up when they smell a cover up. It turns out there's far more than one priest and one victim - some of the true stories told by the victims as the reporters uncover the facts are truly horrendous and gut-wrenching. Definitely not easy to hear, as you know it has happened in real life, and probably hundreds of thousands of times over the last century.

How Ruffalo is only up for Best Supporting Actor, and not Best Actor, is past me! McAdams, on the other hand, is not that utilised - both due to the ensemble cast, I guess. Keaton and Schreiber are good, as is Tucci as the crusading small-time lawyer, but Ruffalo really steals the show, with his heart on the line and it shows in his performance. It's really a great film about newspaper reporting, but is told so well and deals with such an important topic that it is actually enjoyable to watch everyone excel - including director McCarthy, who already has form with 'Win Win'. Certainly not "fun", but a great film.

A hard-hitting, factual, and emotional ride that doubles as a look into how the field of investigative journalism for print used to work. The Spotlight team (a four person intensive investigative journalist team for The Boston Globe) stumbles upon the conspiracy/cover-up of the century when they investigate a sexual abuse claim involving a catholic priest and discover that this kind of thing has been going on for decades, involves many more priests than originally expected, and it goes all the way up to the top of the Catholic church. This is more of an ensemble film, and our leads do fantastic jobs. Mark Ruffalo (Who slowly boils over into a raw, intense, driven, emotional performance) is Mike Rezendes, Rachel McAdams is Sacha Pfeiffer, Michael Keaton is Walter "Robby" Robinson (the editor and head of the Spotlight team), and Brian d'Arcy James (Who also portrayed Shrek on Broadway. He blends seamlessly into his role here) is Matt Carol. They all shine as our Spotlight team. Liev Schriber as new editor Marty Baron (The man who sets it all into motion by assigning the Spotlight team onto the story), Stanley Tucci as Mitchell Garabedian (A lawyer who had filed some of the first claims of sexual abuse against the catholic church), and John Slattery as Ben Bradley Jr. are fantastic as well. Some of the imagery is a bit haunting (plenty of shots of Catholic churches that loom over both our heroes and suburban houses), and there are a surprising amount of moments where the floor drops out from under you as the true scope and extent of the damage is revealed (A great example is the closing text crawl that left my jaw dropped in horror). Spotlight sheds light on one of the most important news stories of the past several decades, and it is to be commended for tackling it's subject material with passion while still remaining faithful to the truth of the story. Simply put: Spotlight is an incredible film. It's enough to make you mourn the death of print journalism.

This journalistic drama recounts a pivotal 12 months of an investigative research team from the Boston Globe, who uncovered decades of systematic abuse against children by the Catholic Church. With subject matter so infuriating and gut-wrenching, it would have been easy for writer-director Tom McCarthy to create a good versus evil arc and give the audience a clear-cut bad guy to despise and deplore. But McCarthy opts for a more intelligent route and keeps the individual offending priests faceless (barring one unsettling and revelatory scene), instead homing in on the atrocities committed by the institution. Unravelling like a journalistic thriller sans the glee, Spotlight is an insightful, methodical and utterly compelling film that provides a window not only into the earth-shattering monstrosities at its core, but also into the mechanics and minutiae of old-school reporting. Understanding that the interactions between the key players is critical to maintaining a level of reality in what would otherwise seem completely unbelievable (despite being true), McCarthy keeps his direction unflashy, allowing the high calibre cast to flourish. Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Brian d'Arcy James, Live Schreiber, John Slattery and Stanley Tucci are all at the top of their games with fleshed out and layered performances that favour subtlety over grandstanding. Spotlight is a brilliantly told true story that captivates from beginning to end, deserving each of its six Academy Award nominations and a place on everybody's must-see list.

I didn't realize just how much this film was connecting with me until they reached the end of the film and gave some of the aftermath facts.  Suddenly, I was involuntarily weeping.  I think it was just the combination of the victim interviews that the investigators engage in throughout the film, and then their articulation of my own frustration with the entire system.  It all compounded to connect with me in ways I never expected.  I cannot recommend Spotlight enough, it was a great film and one that touches on a scandal that is difficult to face, but one that needed to be addressed.

The same could be said for the film industry, but there are always exceptions because for every dozens of films like Alvin and the Chipmunks, we get a Spotlight. Director, Tom McCarthy, takes his time to tell this brilliant true story through a tight script that slowly begins to uncover the truth behind one of the Catholic Church's greatest cover-ups. It is a reminder of how important good journalism can be in today's world. Hopefully after watching Spotlight more people will begin reading their news from trusty newspapers instead of simply reading headlines from any internet article. It was refreshing to see a film like this portraying what good journalism is all about without taking any shortcuts. As a communication major the subject matter really appealed to me and I felt very emotional during a couple of scenes. McCarthy did a fantastic job at going through the every day ordeal of investigating. If you notice there is barely any reference towards these characters backgrounds or their family life. The entire film focuses entirely on their profession and that is what makes this such a powerful film because it avoids any kind of manipulation into character development. I loved the attention to detail that McCarthy brought to the film and how he decided to exclusively build it all around the investigation.

Bringing the true events of an investigation concerning the child molestation cover-up by the Catholic Church to life in a film might not seem like an interesting subject matter, but McCarthy handles the material with grace. He manages to slowly build the tension by going through the everyday ordeals of serious journalism. Spotlight is the name given to the investigative section of the Globe comprised of four reporters that take their time to research an important issue and build a compelling story. In this case they discover a link between several child molestation incidents with some priests from the Boston area and how the Church has repeatedly covered up for them by simply relocating them to other areas. These four reporters are given the gigantic task of trying to unmask this secretly huge system of defense built by the Catholic Church. The film accomplishes what it sets out to do from the first frame and it delivers one of the best films about investigative journalism in years. 

This is a team effort, there are no lead performances in this film. Michael Keaton might be the leader of the Spotlight team, but Mark Ruffalo, Rachel McAdams, and Brian d'Arcy James all deliver strong performances. Ruffalo has received much of the acclaim because he has some of the more emotional moments on screen, and that verbal standoff off with Keaton is powerful, but everyone on screen delivers solid performances. Liev Schreiber is also outstanding as the new editor in chief who arrives at the Globe and comes up with the idea for the story. And Stanley Tucci of course is always mesmerizing any time he's on screen. Spotlight has probably my favorite ensemble cast of the year. I was a huge fan of this film and of course comparisons with All The President's Men are justified.

By Ricky Miller
I am rarely left speechless when I go to the movies. 
"Spotlight" was one of the exceptions.  In this based-on-truth story, to see, let alone hear about what happened to young boys,  was reprehensible.  
Michael Keaton headlines as Walter "Robby" Robinson, head of a team of Boston reporters who band together and spend every moment delving into their story.  Other members of the team include Sacha Pfeiffer (Rachel McAdams),  Mike Rezendes (Mark Ruffalo) and Matt Carroll (Brian d'Arcy James).
The team works feverishly every waking moment at the Boston Globe, where they fight to put the story to bed by the end of the day.
As the story moves on and weaves its tableau, the amount of wrongdoings by various members of the clergy is shocking and downright disgusting.  During the team's inquiry into the Catholic Church, it is surmised that more than 70 higher ups within the church were in the wrong. 
On the lighter side of things, Stanley Tucci ("The Hunger Games") is stellar as attorney Mitchell Garabedian.  When his persona is on the screen, one listens to every nuance and bit of dialogue he utters.
Even McAdams' Sacha character mentions she does not join her grandmother anymore at daily mass for the sheer principal of it all.  Because of the events occurring at the church, Sacha feels that even attending mass would be a slap in the face to all of the victims.  
Also integral to the story is Liev Schreiber's  Marty Baron, the Boston Globe's editor-in-chief.  He wants to know the nitty gritty of it all, down to actual concrete proof.
Filling in the blanks of bureaucracy and all-around corruption are Billy Crudup's Eric Macleish, an attorney representing the Archdiocese of Boston, who was integral in part of the cover-up.
Another person fueling the cover up is Paul Guilfoyle's Pete Conley, who tries to shed various church clergy from embarrassment due to their improprieties.
In the end game of things, this hardcore drama will leave you with a feeling of disbelief and amazement on how this cover-up has gone on for so many years.  
In the end game of things, the Boston Globe walked away with multiple Pulitzer prizes for reporting on incidents that occurred in the city and it turns out all over the world.
Grade:  A

This star studded cast comes together to tell the true story of how the Boston Globe was finally able to breakthrough the decades long wall of silence, and expose the Catholic Church's child molestation scandal. Michael Keaton headlines this all-star cast and shows that while he's been out of the spotlight (pun intended) for some time now, he hasn't lost a beat. As the enigmatic leader of the newspaper's Spotlight section, Walter Robinson (Keaton) will not give up the fight for the truth, no matter the personal cost. Even when his own bosses tell him the story is dead and to give up, he refuses to let it go and he shows that one man with a mission really can change the world. This film doesn't simply shine a light on the Catholic Church in a way it would rather nobody ever had, but it also gives views an in depth, inside look at all the intricacies that go into investigative journalism. With all the reports of fake news and all of us who simply get our news from staring at a screen, it's hard to think about all the effort that goes into getting that information from real life to print and I personally found the process fascinating. This film has a lot going for it, from an inside look at a long forgotten industry to the mysteries behind a long hidden secret. It features some terrific writing and more than one outstanding performance. You don't get six Oscar nominations by accident. This is a great film and a great addition to our list of can't miss movies!

"It takes a village to raise a child. It takes a village to abuse one too". . . Haunting words spoken from a film that has now put the Catholic church under fire like never before. Back in 2001, the world was shocked in an instant when an evil force took a couple of planes and showed the American culture how delusionally safe we really were. But while the dust and destruction of 9/11 seemingly overshadowed the world, a crack team of investigative journalists from the Boston Globe were planning on shining some light on another evil that had been secretly preying on our people for years. "Spotlight" was the Boston Globe's journalism branch that took this monster on. . . Their mission, to break down the battle tested defensive walls of the Catholic church and expose a protected ring of child molestation that had been going on for how long, nobody knows. With the church's claws in the community and the courts alike, this team would have to stop at nothing to hit their mark. Turn every stone, track down each victim they could find, push the buttons of the powers that be, and show a level of perserverence when it seemed like the world would be against them. What they found in the end was nothing anybody could have fathomed. The shepards do indeed tend to their flocks, but what happens when you find an entire pack of wolves dressed in shepard's clothing???
	I can tell why the church is pissed about this piece of work. If they had a heavy hand in trying to quash the initial story, the now critically acclaimed film depicting their fateful attempt in doing so must pose as a kill shot to their general perception now. And if any of this is true, which many sources are pointing to be the case, it is simply maddening. The level of protection and enablement by a system dedicated to the serving of good, the denial of the public that follows suit, and the lack of accountability sentenced on those found guilty. This film is duely well done and serves as another punch to the gut reminder of how the human race has descended to hell in a hand basket. Directing, acting, and a beautifully ominous score serve as high notes to this wonderfully told scandal. My only qualm comes from the writing and adaptation of the story, which I found lacking in the conflict it was promising. For how threatened this team was for trying to wage war on an enemy they were told would stop at nothing to shut their efforts down, we didn't see much of that backlash as the team seemed to really put things in motion once they connected the dots. We didn't see that "hell hath no fury who poses a threat to the Catholic Church" that we all would expect. For that, the conflict and resolution of the film seemed rather casual and hitting light on points that should be much more emotionally scarring. It was a minor blemish to an otherwise rather beautiful model of one of the ugliest stories to rock our culture these past many years. "Spotlight" shines bright and should finish a close third to The Big Short and The Revenant for best movie of 2015.

'Spotlight' is a Drama/Biopic that tells the true story of the Boston Globe reporting team known as 'Spotlight' and their investigations into the allegations of child abuse in the Catholic Church and how what they uncovered in Boston had a huge affect on the rest of the world. This isn't a topic that people really like to discuss openly and is something that happened fairly recently and is still having an impact on society today. And this film did an amazing job at presenting this story in a way that makes it easy to understand for the audience and keeps it very grounded and real without making it a very uncomfortable thing to watch. It is impossible to tell the story without having to go into some of the horrifying and somewhat confronting details, so the film did great at finding a balance between being too controversial and being too Hollywood. That aside, this movie was very well put together through multiple departments. The acting was fantastic as is expected from a cast of fantastic actors and actresses, Tom McCarthy did an astounding job directing the film rather surprisingly, the writing was exceptional and it really is a big Best Picture contender. 

The performances in this film were just so damn amazing to see. Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Liev Shreiber, Stanley Tucci, and John Slattery all killed it in their roles. This was probably the best ensemble cast of the year as everyone was fully committed and delved deep into their roles to the point where you stop noticing that it is Keaton and Ruffalo. Amongst all the greatness, Mark Ruffalo was still the stand-out performance of the film, watching him act in this film makes me wonder why the guy isn't a bigger actor than he is. It is a shame that most people only think of The Hulk when you mention Ruffalo as he has other roles where he puts in some solid performances. Michael Keaton as always was great, he is one of the best working today so you just know he is going to nail any role you give him. Unfortunately because of the other amazing performances around him he couldn't stand out enough to get a Best Actor nomination but he was very entertaining nonetheless. 

The directing by Tom McCarthy was a surprise for me after i had looked at his previous work. I was unfamiliar with his 3 earlier films so really all i had to go on was last years 'The Cobbler' and well, it didn't have me really excited to see how he does on this film at all. But after seeing the amazing work he did with this film, it is hard to say that the same guy who directed 'The Cobbler' also directed the Best Picture nominated 'Spotlight'. The way he ties this film together and arranges all of the individual stories going on was very impressive to see. For quite a bit of the film you have the various characters all going off and investigating certain aspects of the case, and to be able to follow each one of their journeys in a way that allows you to keep track of everyone and not get lost is a great achievement. I also like the way he paced the film, there were a couple of moments fairly early on where i felt it could pick up the speed a little, but after 30 minutes in it was smooth sailing. But when much of the scenes involve interviews, meetings and scenes of those sorts it is very difficult to try and cover everything without skipping things or boring people, so well done again. 

So in the end, Spotlight is just an amazing movie and manages to remain entertaining for the entire 2 hour runtime. It provides you with many of the facts and information regarding the allegations and mixes that in with a very interesting and entertaining story and film. The performances are all great and definitely worth watching just to see these great actors doing what they do best. I love a good biopic and this is definitely one of them so i highly recommend checking it out. Will it win Best Picture? Although my pick is still 'The Revenant' i would have to say this one of the top 3 nominated that actually has a chance.

A proper film about proper journalism, Spotlight is an account of the Boston Globe's investigation into the activities of paedophile catholic priests. What they uncover is a sickening and shocking amount of abuse by predatory priests that was covered up for decades by the upper echelons of the church and the wider establishment. A difficult and harrowing tale, the subject is beautifully handled by director Tom McCarthy. The plot focuses very much on the tight knit investigative "Spotlight" team, who are tasked to work on long running, in-depth stories. This four person team, headed by editor Walter Robinson uncovers the unbelievable scale of the abuse and the lengths people went to in order to hush things up. Based on the incredible true story of how the Boston Globe uncovered the massive scandal of child molestation and cover-up within the local Catholic Archdiocese, Spotlight manages to deliver a fantastic retelling of the story with very well execution, a very intense theme, and a cast of charming and unforgettable characters with an all-star cast to go with it. For years, there have been so many movies about people trying to uncover huge scandals and most of these movies have failed to make themselves likeable, and then suddenly, Spotlight comes in and shows these other movies how a true story is supposed to be retold properly!!! I highly doubt that I will ever see a movie this engaging and enjoyable as Spotlight, but the one thing I know for sure, is that this is definitely one of 2015's best movies ever.

Spotlight is based on true events and stars Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Mark Ruffalo, John Slattery, Brian d'Arcy James, and Liev Schreiber as employees of the Boston Globe who uncovered the story of Catholic priests molesting children and covering up the evidence with help from high-ranking Cardinals. The film was nominated for six Academy Awards, winning Best Original Screenplay and Best Picture. What else is there to say about a movie with that prestige?

To start, the cast is great. Mark Ruffalo (who was nominated for Best Supporting Actor) really shines. Liev Schreober, playing the editor of the Globe, is the initial driving force that gets the ball rolling. Stanley Tucci delivers a humbling and troubled performance as a lawyer who has defended many victims of this abuse. There isn't a poorly-given performance or an annoying character in this entire movie, which is refreshing.

It's the little things that really carry the load here, however. Howard Shore (Lord of the Rings franchise) composes a beautiful, melodic, and at times haunting score, appropriately accompanying the tone of the film. Speaking of tone, major props to McCarthy! With this story, it would have been easy to approach it in a melodramatic way, but he directs a very respectful film here. The pacing of the movie is also very consistent. My dad said "there was never really a lull," and I agree. The movie just keeps snowballing, getting bigger and more urgent.

Now, I do have a couple tiny nit-picks with this movie. There's a little bit of journalism jargon I didn't understand at first because the words were used in a way that gave no information to their meanings, but it became clearer as time progressed. Hey! Speaking of progressing time, there was really no clear indication about how time passed in this movie. In one scene, they mention how the Spotlight story had been put to the side for six weeks because of 9/11. There was a montage scene later on depicting the further passing of time, but the random jumps felt odd with no explanation.

Folks, this movie won Best Picture for a reason. When you combine a true story with a cast like this, the odds are ever in your favor (remember 12 Years a Slave?) If you enjoy movies based on true events or just good movies in general, go watch Spotlight today (ON NETFLIX!)

Final rating: A-

-Spotlight is een 2015 Amerikaanse biografische drama film geregisseerd door Tom McCarthy en geschreven door McCarthy en Josh Singer. De film volgt de Boston Globe's "Spotlight"-team, de oudste continu werkende krant inlichtingendienst in de Verenigde Staten,en haar onderzoek naar gevallen van wijdverbreide onrust en seksueel misbruik van kinderen in de omgeving van Boston door talrijke rooms-katholieke priesters. Het is gebaseerd op een reeks verhalen door de echte Spotlight Team die de Globe 2003 Pulitzer Prize voor openbare dienstverlening verdiende.De film sterren Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, John Slattery, Stanley Tucci, Brian d'Arcy James, Liev Schreiber en Billy Crudup.

-Spotlight werd getoond in de competitie van het 72e Internationale Filmfestival van Venetië. En werd ook getoond bij het Telluride Film Festival en de speciale presentaties gedeelte van de 2015 Toronto International Film Festival. De film werd uitgebracht op 6 november 2015, door Open Road Films. Hij won vele vakkundige en critici' association awards en werd uitgeroepen tot een van de beste films van 2015 door verschillende publicaties.

--Kritische reactie:

-Bij de herziening aggregator Rotten Tomatoes de film heeft een score van 96%, gebaseerd op 201 reviews, met een gemiddelde score van 8.9/10. De site's kritische consensus luidt: "Spotlight gaat probleemloos om met de sensationele bijzonderheden omtrent haar feiten gebaseerde verhaal terwijl ze weerstaat voor de verleiding om fêteren zijn helden, resulterend in een drama dat eert het publiek én haar real-life onderwerpen." Op Metacritic, heeft de film een score van 93 uit 100, gebaseerd op 44 critici, met vermelding "succes."
-Variëty's Justin Chang noemde de film "een prachtig geregeld en fascinerende gedetailleerde uiteenzetting van de Boston Globe's Pulitzer Prize-winnend onderzoek naar de wijdverbreide pedofilie schandalen en latere cover-ups binnen de Katholieke Kerk".

-Bij de 2015 Toronto International Film Festival, Spotlight finishte als derde in de kijkers stemming  voor het People's  Choice Award.

-- Reacties uit de katholieke kerk:

-Kardinaal Sean O'Malley van het aartsbisdom Boston zei Spotlight illustreert hoe de krant verslaggeving aanmoedigde  de kerk "te behandelen wat was beschamend en verborgen." Vatican Radio, officiële radio dienst van de Heilige Stoel, noemde het "eerlijke" en "dwingende" en zei dat het hielp de Amerikaanse katholieke kerk "volledig te aanvaarden de zonde, toe te geven in het openbaar en alle gevolgen van dien te betalen." Luca Pellegrini op de Vaticaanse Radio website schreef dat de Globe reporters "maakten zichzelf voorbeelden van hun meest pure roeping , dat van vinden van de feiten, verifiëren bronnen en zichzelf makend--- voor het welzijn van de Gemeenschap en van een stad--- strijders van de noodzaak voor rechtvaardigheid."

Watching Spotlight before its Best Picture Academy Award. I found myself both infused, yet off the boil. It isn't that this film is bad. That couldn't be much further from the truth. The main problem here is that it is packed to the rafters with dialogue. It does hold the interest of the viewer, but watching this, I can only think of how much this perhaps should have been a book rather than a film. Having said that, as a film this is high-quality cinema, well put together and pure solid gold. Shining a spotlight over one of the darkest things imaginable. This film is not particularly original in its format, but it is in the way it goes about telling you its story. You could just listen to this and be equally as happy and I don't know what I should think about that. I sat in the chair and was completely sucked into this film, and as I left the cinema, I felt as though I had been shocked ("shocked". The age of the understatement). Shocked more by the true story rather than the actual film. Although, as I thought about this film more and more; I became aware that I liked this film a lot more than I first thought. If the story is shocking, the film is putting that story in coherent form and harnessing that shock. The film plays as a narration of the finding of evidence and the actual confrontations in this film are few and far between; I can only think of one or two solid confrontations that actually made me recoil. The steady growth of this film makes it incredible. Far from boring, but for some reason slightly unfulfilling. Maybe the subject matter is to blame for that. Maybe I just need to watch this again. I feel as though I am understating this film, but the truth is, I haven't actually made my mind up on this one.

See yourself in these character's and recognize some of humanities flaws. No heroes, just humans. Working shock and intrigue into a tight, but somehow messy, yet all the more satisfying and saddening bundle. Really, the single members of this cast cannot be mentioned on their own. For each of the cast members plays as well as the next. A true ensemble of true actors, playing true characters, in a true film. Perfection on the performance front. You won't even find yourself thinking about it, and that is a high compliment for such a film that hones on the truly horrific details of the story-line and paying off when needed. I would have loved to see more back and forth between these performers though. As mentioned before, the confrontations here are few and far between and could have given the film a different fold to slip down.

Spotlight is perfection on all levels, but the fact it has been put on screen. Sometimes, some things just work better on the page. Prepare for a bumpy ride. Prepare to be disgusted. Prepare to feel... As long as a film can make you do that, then it has worked on some level. Spotlight, I salute you. You had me on the edge of my seat, whilst burying me inside of it. I hope I haven't buried you six feet under in this review.

This year's Oscar frontrunner for best picture deals with The Boston Globe newspaper's expose of the dirty dealings and hypocrisies of the Catholic Church. More specifically it hones in on the sexual molestation of young boys by Catholic priests. However, despite this controversial hot potato of a subject the film seriously lacks any raw power or urgency. Instead it is content to have its leading investigators amble from meeting to meeting obtaining information rather too easily. Things aren't helped by the lack of an emotional hook. The victims interviewed are all adults and come across as basic stock characters shouldering all the worst lines of dialogue like 'Who can say no to god'. Lines like this are so phony that one winces with embarrassment. Anyone who has seen 'All the President's Men' or Netflix's current 'Making a Murderer' will know that films exposing evil or corruption can be nerve jinglingly tense and emotively powerful, but Mark Ruffalo's annoying depiction of righteous anger just doesn't cut it. Where the film does succeed is in keeping viewer interest in a subplot as to who in Spotlight's department was responsible, and therefore complicit, in burying the story years earlier. Performance wise the Oscar nominated turns of both Ruffalo and Rachel McAdams seem quite conventional and uninteresting, whereas the actors in smaller parts; Liev Schreiber, Stanley Tucci, Billy Crudup and John Slattery all fare much better. The 'Spotlight', however, does shine on one person; Michael Keaton. For an actor who is often guilty of being way over the top he is here at his most understated. It is more than fair to say that he single handedly elevates 'Spotlight' to a level way above the mediocrity of the rest of the film.

"Spotlight" tells the true story of the 2001 investigation by the Boston Globe into the Catholic Church's child molestation scandal. ("Spotlight" is the name of the Globe's investigative reporting team.) 

The story begins with Marty Baron (Liev Shreiber) taking over as the Globe's new editor.  At the time, there was a minor case alleging that an archbishop named Cardinal Law was engaged in a cover-up in which he shuffled priests accused of pedophilia from parish to parish while continuing to allow them to work with children. While such rumblings were nothing new, the paper had never really pursued them in deference to Boston's powerful Catholic Church. But Baron, being a Jewish outsider, instructs the team to launch an all-out investigation. 

Normally I'm not a big docudrama fan but this movie feels a lot more "docu" than drama. I had a little bit of a hard time keeping all of the names straight and got tripped up just about every time someone mentioned Cardinal Law, thinking it was some sort of legal term. 

Though the legal maneuverings involving sealed documents are somewhat interesting, the movie is at its best when the victims tell their stories. Mark Ruffalo is particularly good as one of the reporters and Rachel McAdams is pretty convincing as well. The beauty of this film is that despite being jam-packed with big name Hollywood stars, all of the performances are all low-key and believable.

This is one of those rare times when walking into the theater with low expectations really paid off for me.  "Spotlight" is both educational and engrossing, as any good documentary should be. The fact that it's actually a drama makes this quite a feat.

Well it took me a few months, but I finally got around to watching Spotlight. I don't think I could have seen this film soon enough. Director Tom McCarthy crafted an absolute master piece here. Watching this film I experienced shock, disgust, anger, and bewilderment. But McCarthy didn't force these emotions upon me. No, he did the exact opposite, and that is what is so brilliant about this film.

Spotlight is based on a true story and chronicles a team of journalists working for The Boston Globe who investigate widespread systematic child sexual abuse within the confines of the Catholic church. Through their investigation they come into contact with several victims of abuse, as well as lawyers and members of the Catholic clergy that helped cover up these awful events.

Knowing that the content in this film actually occurred in real life horrified me. McCarthy is absolutely aware of the fact that this is how much of the audience will feel when they watch this film. McCarthy knows this is a true story, and he uses that to his absolute advantage in his directorial style. Everything about this film is so subdued and real. Watching this didn't feel like watching a movie. It felt like watching a documentary, and I mean that in the best way possible.

McCarthy revels in the mundane with Spotlight. This could have easily turned into a generic thriller, fabricating events to play up the drama of the entire situation, trying to show the Catholic church go after the team of journalists as they continue to uncover more and more of the church's disgusting secrets. But no, McCarthy doesn't do that. Instead he focuses on the small quiet moments between the investigators and victims of abuse, as well as the frustrations they go through when trying to navigate legal red tape. There is no real danger or threat to the protagonists of this film. These journalists aren't heroes, they are simply a group of people doing their job, trying the best they can to bring these horrific acts to light.

Because this story feels so real and authentic, the stories of child abuse and the Catholic Church's cover up are so much more powerful than if McCarthy had over dramatized the situation. The outrage I felt watching Spotlight is unlike anything I have ever felt watching a film before.This is especially punctuated by the fact that this film has no real emotional outbursts or catharsis of its own, sans one or two scenes where it felt absolutely justified. It allows the audience to feels these emotions on their own, instead of showing it to them. Everything about this film is understated, and that is what makes it so effective.

This muted style of McCarthy translates to equally subdued performances from the cast, and everyone knocks it out of the park. Mark Ruffalo gives a standout performance, transforming into the character of Michael Rezendes, so much so that at times I honestly forgot that I was watching Ruffalo portray a character, I was that invested in his story. The same can be said for the rest of the cast as well. Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Liev Schreiber, and Stanley Tucci all give equally great performances, but none of them completely disappear into their character quite like Ruffalo did. There is no real  Everyone plays off each other so well that I did not feel like I was watching a group of actors giving amazing performances, I felt I was watching a group of real people dealing with a real and horrific situation.

The cinematography in the film is nothing spectacular, it's actually quite ordinary. This works in the context of the film however, as it continues to reinforce McCarthy's  remarkable ability to show restraint in his directing. There are no real directorial flourishes you would find in this film if someone like a David Fincher or Danny Boyle had directed it. Like everything else in this film, the way it shot is indistinct, if unremarkable, preventing any distraction from the events that are taking place in the film, and giving focus to the real life consequences of the film.

The film captures something so raw and real that by the end of it when the credits roll, and it lists all the cities in the world that have been effected by Catholic cover ups I was left speechless. This film had such an effect on me that I'm still reeling from it even as I write this review. I absolutely loved this film, but I'm not sure if I can say that it is an enjoyable experience.

cinegeek.de Eine Zeitungsmeldung in Boston aus dem Jahr 2002: Über Jahre erlaubte die Kirche den Priestern die Misshandlung von Kindern. Verfasst von Michael Rezendes, einem Mitglied des Spotlight Teams war der Artikel der Beginn einer Reihe von Enthüllungen. Kardinal Bernard Law musste sich schliesslich öffentlich entschuldigen und bekam als "Strafe" eine Position in Rom, dort wo er heute noch arbeitet. Tom McCarthys Film Spotlight folgt den Ereignissen, die Boston erschütterten. Spotlight ist einer der grössten Journalisten Filme geworden und darf sich einreihen in die Liste der Klassiker des Genres. Angeführt wird das Spotlight Team von Walter "Robby" Robinson (Michael Keaton) und den drei Reportern Michael Rezendes (Mark Ruffalo), Sacha Pfeiffer (Rachel McAdams) und Matty Carroll (Brian d'Arcy James). Alle Reporter kommen aus Boston und haben selbst irgendwelche Verbindungen zur katholischen Kirche. Ins Rollen wird die Geschichte gebracht von einem Mann, der nicht aus Boston kommt: Marty Baron (Liev Schreiber). Er stösst auf mögliche Vertuschungen und beruft das Spotlight Team in sein Büro. Wir lernen den privaten Hintergrund der Journalisten kennen. Sie alle gehören zu der Sorte Mensch, die mehr Zeit mit den Kollegen verbringen als mit den eigenen Familien. Es sind Leute, die wir kennen und verstehen. Zunächst liegt der Fokus auf dem Priester John J. Geoghan, der Jahre zuvor Kinder missbrauchte. Früh wird aber auch deutlich, dass es sich hier um mehr als nur einen faulen Priester handelt. Den Journalisten wird bewusst, dass sie es mit einem organisierten System von Korruption zu tun haben. Es stellt sich die Kardinalfrage: Wusste Bernard Law davon? Während Sacha und Michael die Opfer der Kirche interviewen, erleben wir die Stadt Boston: Wir tauchen ein in verschiedene stark voneinander abgegrenzte Bezirke, "Klassen". Die Strassen von Boston wirken noch so, als ob die Kolonialzeit nie geendet hätte. Hier sitzen die Männer zusammen, trinken Kaffee oder essen Hot Dog und sprechen über die Arbeit. Obwohl ich nie in Boston war, wirkt das Szenrario auf mich echt und das ist wichtig. Der Film geht einer tieferen Wahrheit nach. Hier wird nicht nur das Trauma der Opfer aufgearbeitet, sondern der gesamten Gemeinde. Vertrauen und Glauben ist der Schlüssel zum Film, den McCarthy sehr ernst nimmt. Mark Ruffalo verkörpert das wie kein Zweiter, wenn er wie ein Wahnsinniger in die kirchlichen Gemächer vordringt; er der selbst vor Jahren seinen Glauben verlor. Spotlight wird hier zu einem Rache Film. Nicht zuletzt wird auch deutlich, wie wichtig guter Journalismus ist. Spotlight mit all seinem Leid und seiner Dringlichkeit wirkt da wie ein notwendiger Aufruf!

The team is now basically in conflict in the church as their list of suspected dirty priests blows up from one to eighty seven. Rightly regarded as one of the finest films of 2015, Spotlight is an intelligent and compelling look at one of the biggest deceptions of the 21st century. A witty and often biting script cuts to the core of investigative journalism and the true effects of systemic abuse, and an impeccable cast brings the characters to life. Every actor is on top form, and none more so than Mark Ruffalo. So fantastic as the troubled Hulk in the Avengers, here we seem him truly transforming into a bright, ambitious, resourceful but also emotionally driven and occasionally overzealous reporter. The way he moves, speaks and even his facial expressions, everything he does convinces you that he is 100% invested in this role.
This is certainly a very wordy movie, with much being said and analysed, and often at a rapid pace. But it works because the story is constantly being advanced and new developments are always being made. Issues such as the deep dependence on the Church and the harmful consequences that such a blind faith can have make up the backbone of the story, but the movie never makes the mistake of being a cheap finger poke at religion, fully acknowledging that the issue is the abuse of power employed by those within its ranks, and not the institution itself, that causes the damage. The facts the movie reveals are truly shocking, and its final moments will leave you stunned. Spotlight is a solid piece of cinema, rooted in fact and flowering in the minds of its viewers.

Spotlight is a tremendous piece of film making that will make you go completely speechless. The movie is a dramatization of the Boston Globe newspaper's 'Spotlight' section who, in 2001, began an investigation into the systematic child abuse by Catholic priests in the Boston Diocese going back over a (known) period of 20 years. Unraveling the abuse also reveals a huge conspiracy by the Catholic Church (including the current Cardinal) to cover up said abuse by exercising their influence in both political and legal circles, buying off those who were abused and come forward, using gagging orders and confidentiality agreements to make sure the truth never comes to light. 
Tom McCarthy knows how to set up the sensitive subject, it attempts to "fairly" represent the Church's side in the beginning. We start with one incident of sexual assault, or rather the aftermath. It's a short scene and it doesn't show a mother weeping over her victimized child praying for the blood of the Pope, while a priest twists his handle bar mustache. This scene cleverly, and deceitfully, shows this as a one-time incident that the church regrets happened. 
The acting here is phenomenal. Michael Keaton, Mark Ruffalo, Rachel McAdams, Liev Schreiber, John Slattery, Billy Crudup, Stanley Tucci, Brian d'Arcy James, Neal Huff, Paul Guilfoyle, Len Cariou, and the list goes on. Everybody who had any single line in this film was great. This film is built around the powerful performances delivered by these talented people and the passion their real life counterparts brought to their job, which really shines through. This film has power in spades and as the onion is peeled back, you are left stunned at this true story. A film that makes you overwhelmed and needing a long bath to try and cleanse all the grime of the world off of you, Spotlight is a great work that deserves all of its forthcoming accolades.
The movies biggest strength is its story telling  which is a master class. The way McCarthy builds up the tension is incredibly intelligent, so that in the end, it all falls down onto you. I expected this movie to be shocking and making me feel uneasy, but then it gave me a lot more: compassion, in a way I never expected. Absolutely loved it. There was no unnecessary drama, the movie focuses solely on the issue of the controversial story it tells so well. The emotional impact of this movie is so significant because of the reality that surrounds the actual cases that are portrayed. 
The film suffers from a few pacing issues during the first act but quickly recovers and doesn't slow down. The reality of the story being told is what makes this movie essential to watch. The importance of the issues discussed throughout is never understated and every character plays their role to perfection in contributing to the unfolding of this unique and true series of events. Religion plays a role in this narrative as it naturally contrasts and opposes the scandalous nature of the cases highlighted in this movie. Religion and morality are constants throughout the film as they compliment the nuanced narrative and contrast the tragedy being focused on. 
Spotlight is an important film that deserves to be acknowledged for the role it plays in communicating the significance of a substantial and controversial story in need of attention and ongoing in the world even today.

The true story of how, in 2001, reporters at the Boston Globe investigated accusations of Catholic priests in Boston molesting children.  Following on from leads, interviews with victims, existing court cases and extensive research they reveal decades of abuse.  Moreover, they discover that the issue was far wider spread than they at first believed, that senior members of the diocese were aware of the issue and that the church systemically covered up the crimes.

A well made movie: interesting and intriguing.  It had the potential to degenerate into a dull, dry paint-by-numbers docudrama but writer-director Tom McCarthy gives the characters depth, builds the intrigue like a spy thriller and makes a very realistic-feeling movie about investigative journalism.

The director is aided by some great, understated performances from his cast.  Michael Keaton is the pick of the bunch but Mark Ruffalo, Liev Schreiber, Rachel McAdams, John Slattery, Brian dArcy James and Stanley Tucci put in solid performances too.

Another factor the movie has in its favour is timing: (alleged) abuse of children by priests of the Catholic church is a highly charged, highly publicized, internationally widespread, current issue.  While I do not think Spotlight was the best film of 2015 (for me, that honour goes to The Big Short), Spotlight isn't far behind the best in terms of pure cinematic quality plus it taps into a highly topical issue.  

I thus think it is the contemporary nature of its subject matter that saw it edge out the competition for the Best Picture Oscar in 2016, and I don't see a problem in that (despite my preference for The Big Short).  One of the purposes of art is to capture the look, feel and issues of the times and preserve them for posterity.  Spotlight fulfils this function very well.

I had really hoped that "Spotlight" would live up to the hype of 6 Oscar nominations and its status as the front runner for Best Picture.  It did not.  Expectations aside, I found this film to be interesting and well-done but not at the same level of Oscar contenders like "The Revenant," "Room," and "The Martian."  The only nomination that I would have given to this film is to Tom McCarthy for his screenplay and its treatment of this sensitive subject matter.  The statistics are shocking and the stories of the victims are sad but the film never seems like an attack on the church.  The use of strong sexual language is limited to the first half of the movie, serving as a reference point that we can remember throughout the story without having to hear those words over and over again.  I think that the shock of hearing some of those terms is necessary to grasp the levity of the allegations but I appreciate that the script didn't continually hit us over the head with graphic sexual explanations.  The film focuses on exploring investigative journalism instead of pushing a hidden agenda, and it is impressive that a story about new research could be so riveting.  The acting is above average, especially the Boston accents, but I disagree with the Oscar nominations of Rachel McAdams and Mark Ruffalo in the Supporting categories.  In fact, I enjoyed the acting of Stanley Tucci, Michael Keaton, and John Slattery more than either of them.  Ruffalo gets to shine in one emotional scene but his acting throughout the rest of the film is average when compared by this year's performances by Steve Carrell and Idris Elba.  I'm not even sure what stood out about McAdams' performance to bring her so much acclaim.  Outside of the acting, the atmosphere and sense of authenticity adds to the realism of the story.  It was appropriate to film on location at The Boston Globe where the Spotlight team's findings transpired.  "Spotlight" is a very good movie that handles sensitive events in a creative, informative, and nearly unoffensive way.  Just prepare yourself for two hours of depression and a film that may fall below your expectations for an Oscar contender.
