As I've watched an ever-increasing number of films across a variety of genres, I've come to the conclusion that the investigative drama is one of my favorite genres. My favorite movies in this genre are those which are simultaneously low key and suspenseful. Films such as The Third Murder, Rear Window, and The Conversation maintain high levels of tension with a minimum of onscreen violence, achieving the type of audience engagement I'd associate with a high body count thriller with a more measured, intellectual tone. Spotlight is, undoubtedly, one of the best films of the genre I've ever seen. Following the titular "Spotlight" team from The Boston Globe as they investigate what could be the biggest story of their career, a child abuse scandal involving the Catholic Church, the film is extremely tense, yet simultaneously low key, creating an extremely engaging drama without sacrificing the air of authenticity demanded by an adaptation of a true story.

The movie features one of the strongest ensemble casts I have ever seen, to the point that pointing out standouts is very hard because of the inspired performances all around. In a clever bit of directing, these characters are frequently towered over by edifices symbolizing the very organization the team is investigating as they exchange dialogue. This dialogue is engaging not just because of the acting prowess on display, but also because movie also has an excellent script. I particularly like the use of subtext and doublespeak in the film. While the film does not convey as many layers of meaning in a single sentence as Tokyo Story, which I have praised for similar reasons, it acknowledges that it is often counterproductive for a reporter to get accusatory and openly angry with interviewees and that, for the person on the other end of the notepad, threats should not be made openly and publicly, especially towards someone in the position to publish those threats. These are aspects of the profession commonly ignored by films featuring reporters.

I suspect some people will find the film to be anti-religious. I didn't get that impression. Spotlight certainly does not portray the Catholic Church as an institution in a positive manner, but it does not attack its God directly, only the mortals ostensibly in God's service. Throughout the film, the "Spotlight" team conduct repeated telephone interviews with a former Catholic priest who became a critic of the Church due to their handling of sexual abuse claims. He has little positive to say about the people running the church, but still considers himself a Catholic. Even if we assume the existence of an infallible god, humans, those who claim to be servants of that deity may still commit immoral actions, and those acts should not be excused because the evildoer is a priest. Spotlight takes no definite stance on religion, only on those who use it to conceal their own evil acts.

Taking the #1 spot in the list for my favorite films of the decade, this Best Picture winning film shines a light on the extraordinary investigative journalists who revealed one of the most disturbing true secrets that the church had been hiding for many years.

The pinnacle of Investigative Journalist filmmaking

SYNOPSIS:
In 2001, the investigative journalist team, known as "Spotlight", for the Boston Globe gets tasked with digging deep into a potential scandal of the American Church keeping secrets and hiding child molesting priests. Though at first believed to be just a couple "bad apples", the further the team researched, the more they begin to realize that this unimaginable secret is actually being done on a much grander scale.

DIRECTION:
Tom McCarthy really knocks this one out of the park. Every angle is a song and every angle is keeping the right amount of pace while tracking every bit of body language coming off of the phenomenal performances. I've been reviewing many films that aren't asked for an extreme amount of effort on behalf of the directing and I'm compelled to say the same about this film. Despite feeling this way, McCarthy shoots this film in a very particular way where it's hard for me to explain. He is always capturing the right frame at the right moment and whether it's a wide, a medium or a close-up it is particular to a point of perfection. I couldn't imagine the editing nor the direction being any different. I don't want it to be any different. The extreme organization of this film is exquisite and regardless if you're familiar with the true story you're still very much discovering every bit of information along with them. Although I can think of several films of the sort, the only other film I can really compare the meticulous direction with is that of David Fincher's "Zodiac" (2007). 

WRITING:
Every element of this film is damn near flawless for me and the same goes for the writing. As I mentioned in my review of Dark Waters (an also similar film including Mark Ruffalo), when writing a script that is inspired or completely based on true events, you can spot the films that truly do their research. Now, I don't know just how accurate this film is to all of the dialogue that was actually said nor do I know what level of investigation these journalists took on, but anyone can see that this film really dug as deep as it could. A story like this could be scary to tell, especially when it's dealing with an enormous entity like the American Church and so I give the writing and anyone participating in this film in general all of the props in the world.

ACTING:
I'm just going to name all of the noteworthy actors: Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Liv Schreiber, Brian D'Arcy James, John Slattery, Billy Crudup, Stanley Tucci and Mark Ruffalo. Now there are others who played very small roles who were all spectacular, but for this film I really want to narrow this SPECTACULAR lineup to Stanley Tucci and Mark Ruffalo. Stanley Tucci plays one of the most incredible supporting roles to date. He was so integral to the story and every line of dialogue that came out of his mouth felt so true that I nearly forgot he is an actor and I know that's the job and that's how it's supposed to be, but in every scene that he was in I nearly felt I was watching a straight documentary with the real lawyer. He was unbelievable. Moving on we get to Mark Ruffalo. Without having seen all of his films, I can say without a doubt this is the best performance he has every given. It's one of the greatest performances given period. One could argue the best of the decade. Maybe this story is so close to his heart or maybe he just sparked unreal-like empathy, but I felt as though this story affected him to his very core. The emotion was so raw that the whole movie I wanted this story to get out just so I could see himself get closure. I wouldn't be surprised at all that even though Mr. Hulk has smashed through several Marvel films that this was his most emotionally and mentally draining performance he's every had.

CONCLUSION:
All in all, this film goes down as possibly one of my top 10 favorite films of all time. To take a story, entirely filled with dialogue and to keep my interest as much as a Domino's Chocolate Lava Cake, is speaking to significant heights. I can watch this film daily and still be sucked in just as much as the first viewing and the heart wrenching scene between Michael Keaton and Mark Ruffalo. Simply Impeccable. This is a recommend to absolutely everyone. I am a man of faith and for me to still enjoy this film as much as it does, I believe speak volumes.

Spotlight was ok, but devoid of any tension, ambiguity, depth, complexity. We all know the story---the reality---that 90 priests molested and/or had inappropriate sexual interactions with teen and preteens, and that the Catholic Church in Boston and elsewhere covered it up. But this take on that story is about how a principled Jewish editor in chief (played by an apparently bored Liev Schreiber) arrives at the Boston Globe and is the only one who can see injustice and responsible journalism with any clarity, and how it was his moral backbone and intellectual prowess that enabled taking down the Catholic Church when none had dared or been able to do so before--and how many had resisted and/or actively fought against the real story to come out. The acting is uniformly good--it should be; it's a stellar cast--but the whole thing is turned down so low, so drably, so one dimensionally, it is very hard to keep watching and listening to the same lectures over and over (and over and over) for over 2 hours.  There needed to be a reality check--or a devil's advocate--or some other POV beyond the obvious one that is hammered without deviation from the following: molesting children is evil, Catholic priests molested children, the Catholic Church is all over the world, therefore unspeakable evils have unfolded to unfathomable numbers of kids worldwide thanks to the Catholic Church, which must be stopped--and thank goodness for the 100% good, brave, intellectually clean and clear "outsiders" who step forward valiantly to put a stop to evils like Catholicism. Little shortcuts like "Gasp!!! Lawyers who approached the Catholic Church with allegations of abuse for many years did not officially file lawsuits in court?!! Nor did they go to the media?!!! There are nondisclosure agreements with the people who settled with the church---egad!!" Doesn't take into account that 90% of lawsuits against corporations, organizations, universities, and individuals are treated precisely that way. Is it to "cover up what happened," as a conspiracy?  Not necessarily---that is the way that legal action often/usually unfolds--out of court settlements, "mediation," arbitration. And almost always as part of those settlements is a non-disclosure agreement.  It is not unusual--the way this film makes it out to be--that the Catholic Church did something bizarrely untoward each time they were approached with a claim, for their attorneys to work with the plaintiff's attorneys and not to go to the media with it. Not to say the Catholic Church handled--or handles---such things appropriately. But many times in Spotlight actions like the preceding example of settling out of court is conflated with corruption, nefariousness, conspiracy. The Church may be and have been corrupt and nefarious--and even perpetuated conspiracy--but why not climb a bit farther inside it and show how the very people thinking they were doing the right thing were completely wrong-minded about it? THAT in itself is far more arresting and affecting than watching a painfully out of tune children's choir warbe "Silent Night" in a shadowy church, watched over by a priest, while Mark Ruffalo stands in the unwatched darkness, a single tear dribbling down his cheek. Heavy-handed and unnuanced missed opportunity. For an exponentially more effective film on this topic, see "Doubt." That will haunt you. Spotlight, in contrast, will most likely sort of bore you (which you'll then have to deny since it's such a dire topic).

The 2016 Oscar winning Best Picture is an engaging ensemble drama dealing with one of the biggest scandals of this generation. Spotlight is an extremely well paced and insightful look at the work done by the Boston Globe as they discover, investigate and ultimately reveal to the world the decades long cover-up of widespread pedophilia within the priesthood of the Catholic Church.

Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Stanley Tucci, Brian d'Arcy James and Liev Schreiber all deftly inhabit the leading characters they play. This is a major compliment given that there is very little character development. The movie is driven solely by the bigger story. From beginning to end, this movie is guided by one singular linear goal… uncovering the truth and overcoming the obstacles set up to prevent that goal from being accomplished. The only real sub-plot that runs through the film is why it has taken so long for the Globe to look into this story, given the volume of information that it slowly becomes apparent had been provided to them years earlier.

The movie does a fantastic job of illuminating the culture of Boston and the influence that the Boston archdiocese has on the city. It also deals frankly with the sexual nature of the crimes committed, without being exploitative or sensationalist. The reporters know that details are crucial in making sure the public can grasp the enormity of the circumstances. We empathize with the discomfort the reporters experience, but understand the immense value of that discomfort.

The film pays great attention to showing the volume of legwork that was required, especially given that much of it still had to be completed manually in this period when the internet was just at the cusp of becoming a mainstream resource. This movie shows the importance of a free press, but doesn't glorify or oversimplify what goes into making sure that a free press is also a responsible press.  This is a movie I will surely watch again.

Spotlight is based on a true event focusing on the Boston Globe's Spotlight team to research on the systemic Catholic priest child sexual abuse scandals. The team consisting of Michael Rezendez (Mark Ruffalo), Sacha Pfeiffer (Rachel McAdams), Robby Robinson (Michael Keaton), and Marty Baron (Liev Schreiber), interview the abuse victims, research on the perpetrators' priesthood, visit one priest's lawyer Mitch Garabedian (Stanley Tucci), and call psychiatrist Richard Sipe (Richard Jenkins) to puzzle together their story. Just like Dances with Wolves, watching this movie I couldn't help but compare Spotlight to another film about a newspaper company covering a story about a conspiracy with the help of an anonymous informant and the chief-of-staff named Ben Bradlee. Only this time, the journalists from the Washington Post were covering the political scandal at the Watergate hotel. Both All the President's Men and Spotlight were released years after the events occurred, but the latter film came out 14 years after while the former was released four years after. However, Tom McCarthy's film emerged during the heyday of the sexual abuse and rape accusations of Hollywood celebrities, specifically those of Bill Cosby, who lost his 60-year career due to these thousands of reports and was imprisoned 4 years later. Alan Pakula's film came out two years after President Richard Nixon's resignation from the White House for mishandling funds and destroying records. So, does it make Spotlight a rip-off of a classic political thriller or a gripping drama bent on social relevance? While the story does follow the same footprints as All the President's Men, it does have a handful of twists and turns and it's still a well-written film. Maybe The Post will have a new take on the Watergate Scandal.

"Spotlight" is easily 2015's best picture. The film casts Mark Ruffalo,
Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams, and Brian d'Arcy James as the 4 investigative journalists. Each character is comparatively different, but the chemistry on screen fits perfectly.

The movie itself isn't anything special. Its has a dry theme, with a important and worldwide message. However, the film does not ever fail to produce telling an important story that helps overrule the dryness to the film.

The film's setting takes place mostly entirely in Boston. We get to see parts of the then-current Boston Globe offices in Dorchester, Boston, Fenway Park, and the Boston Public Library.

"Spotlight" represents the investigative unit at the Boston Globe.

In the film, the journalists decide to sue the Catholic Church for sealed documents that will help write the story they want to write.

In real life events, as matched with the film, the spotlight team were put down in the sense of rejection/demotivation by people who were victims of the horror, the lawyers who were only doing there job, and the other workers at the Boston Globe.

To the world of Journalism, and the world of news, the story of "Spotlight" is one of the stories that people hope to watch/read. Real news, true journalism, the truth, a movie that exceeds regularity. Expected as it is, this is one of the stories journalists want to tell, its one of the big stories in ones career. Its one of the stories the world doesn't want to hear, especially the people who are very picky on what's written, but those people will read what's being written eventually, and soon will come to find out the truth.

The film emphasizes nobody can get away with child molestation, or any type of abuse. It emphasizes collecting all the facts will certify that justice is done.

During the film we see Michael Keaton's character, the leader of his investigative team fighting his own battles. At some point in the film he says, "we got two stories here, a story about generate clergy, and the story about a bunch of lawyer turning child abuse into a cottage industry, which story do you want us to write? because we're writing one of them." At many points in the film, we see Keaton's character desire to accomplish his goal, to finish the story that needs to be told. We learn that all 4 of the journalist's will keep pushing for the story they need to tell.

The goal, the objective is front and center. There is no hiding what is trying to be done, the film doesn't try to get the journalist's to look for something they want to research. The horrors that need to be uncovered are present, and they are waiting to be told by a committed investigative team.

Beyond doubt, there is a momentum the film carries as the team of 4 build their case, and uncover the story they know was not taken seriously.

"Spotlight" was shot on a Digital, ARRI ALEXA XT Camera. The film has a runtime of 2 hours and 9 minutes, and has an R rating.

The performance in this film is amazing. We get to feel what its like as a journalist, the struggle, and the desire that news people tend to go through everyday when trying to find a story.

At some point during the film, the conversation of The Boston Globes subscribers was mentioned as 53% catholic readers. Making the story that's being investigated, a potential negative impact on TBG. The problem with news in modern day is people don't want to hear an equal side or neutral news. There may be journalists who tell a story from both sides, but people chose to read news from a source they know that tells them the story from the side they stand on. "Spotlight" does show how certain people in the catholic community have reacted to the paper after being published.

By the end of the film we feel good, we feel thankful that a strong team was put on this investigation. We can understand why people may have felt the way they felt, and potentially what it may have been like as a child to be pestered by a priest in the wrong way. This is a confident, slick, and and celebratory telling of the unsung heroes at the Boston Globe that unleashed a horrifying bombshell across the world revealing the pervasiveness of the Roman Catholic clergy child abuse scandal. It's amazing, shocking, and terrifying and this movie does a fantastic job keeping its wits about it and not fancifying a story that needs no dramatization. The acting is bang on from a utterly stacked cast and the dialogue is magnetizing. Just as much as the Spotlight news story, this movie had to grapple with the journalistic integrity of handling subject matter that affects thousands upon thousands of victims. To my eye and as a former Catholic, Tom McCarthy handles that responsibility with flying colors and made a movie that not only is gripping and well made, but is an important tool of awareness.

This movie stays incredibly accurate to true life events, with only minor alterations (i.e., Sacha Pfeiffer did not interview Rev. Ronald H. Paquin on the front porch; it was Steve Kurkjian; in the living room.) The movie has excellent pacing. I would consider it an equivalent to a "page-turner". Every scene is captivating. The actors do a fantastic job at displaying these tough emotions. Mark Ruffalo has some exquisite emotional expressiveness that is subtle, restrained, but still suffocating. The twisted dichotomy between church and governance is encased in journalism, while still being as informative as any documentary could be, and yet, remains absolutely thrilling.

I find it baffling that I would feel the rush of trying to get paperwork from a courthouse or get excited with people trying to write spreadsheets based on the tedious process of going through ministry records. For some reason, McCarthy did it. Spotlight is a film about exposing priests as child molesters, and the Cardinals, Archbishops, and Bishops defend their younger siblings, getting them out of trouble. The journalists at the Boston Globe are dedicated not just to finding the truth and bring justice to the molester priests but help save future victims of the abusers.
Hollywood doesn't consider authenticity a priority, yet McCarthy sees how it is important to study the film being created. It starts out as a Jewish man purchasing a local newspaper. He decides it would be best for the Boston Globe's spotlight team to expand the knowledge on the molestation cases from priests like Fr. Geoghan. They begin investigating, reading documents, talking to victims, consulting experts and lawyers. They would check facts, confirm them, and re-confirm them. It was a tedious and monotonous. It would be difficult to make this cinematic, but McCarthy used montages to show us their progress overtime. The film is also a visual departure to most of the other films I see these days. The colors are muted, lighting is soft and flat, the music is subtle, and the camera work isn't fancy. The actors don't show exaggerated expressions rather, they focus on realistic faces of frustration. This is to represent the slow, monotonous, and tedious process that the journalists must go through. In the end, they publish the paper and expose the molester priests.
Spotlight is the most authentic film about investigative journalism. There isn't a single moment where someone rushed into the office screaming, "I have proof!" Rather, the journalists soldiered onto heaps of paperwork, finding patterns in the ministry records, talking to lawyers who have fought for the victims, and interviewing the victims themselves. They had to overcome the Church's attempts at hiding documents that are opened to the public. They had to go through clips of previous reports, clips they have buried, and lawyers who refused to talk for career preservation purposes.
Vloggers discredit traditional news sources, calling them biased. This resulted in an image of a man, who mustn't be defined by his father's mistakes, as the sins of the father are not the sins of the son, but also the achievements of the father are also the achievements of the son. Politicians are also trying to take down news giants like ABS-CBN and arrested Rappler founder, Maria Ressa for spreading false news. ABS-CBN and Rappler has been trying to show the dark side of Former President Rodrigo Duterte's campaign in drugs. Vloggers show a brighter side to it, even if it isn't all true. They can get away with this, as they aren't regulated by law to confirm any information they get. Despite all the harsh problems and setbacks, journalism in the Philippines has gotten a victory through Maria Ressa's Nobel Peace Prize in journalism.
Journalists go through a lot. And I think we should give them the credit they deserve. Either by telling an accurate and authentic story of the previously unsung heroes who helped bring justice to molester priests and helped the future victims, or by giving awards and recognition to those who persevere despite the constant setback, like Maria Ressa's Nobel Peace Prize in journalism.

The horrific instances of abuse committed by members of the Catholic Church takes centre stage in this harrowing drama from Tom McCarthy ("Stillwater"). "Spotlight" only details the abuse that occurred in Boston, but McCarthy ends the film with a chilling list of places where other major scandals within the Church have taken place, a list made up of 105 U.S. communities and 101 other locations across the globe.

Mike Rezendes, Walter Robinson, Sacha Pfeiffer, and Matt Carroll are the reporters behind the damning Boston Globe article that recounted the years of abuse perpetrated by members of the Catholic Church in parishes throughout Boston. Taking place over the course of seven months between 2001 and 2002, the film follows the reporters of the Boston Globe's Spotlight team as they investigate the alleged abuse committed by members of the Catholic Church. Speaking to survivors, lawyers and members of the Church, the team uncover a decades-old conspiracy in which the Church willingly covered up the crimes committed by members. What follows is a shocking series of events that not only shook the Catholic Church, but also the religious scene in Boston.

"Spotlight" features knockout performances from its entire ensemble cast, featuring stellar turns from Michael Keaton as Walter Robinson, Mark Ruffalo as Mike Rezendes, and Rachel McAdams as Sacha Pfieffer, with the latter two going on to receive Oscar nominations for their performances. Ruffalo, Keaton and McAdams are joined by a star-studded cast, with Brian d'Arcy James, Liev Schreiber, John Slattery, and Stanley Tucci starring alongside them.

McCarthy and Josh Singer ("The Post") pen the film's Oscar-winning screenplay, taking an incredibly sensitive subject and working it into an effective script that doesn't feel exploitative. The film derives an intense and riveting drama from a distressing issue that is still present in the Catholic Church today, with a harrowing report revealing that there had been 330,000 victims of abuse from 1950-2020 in the French Catholic Church alone.

The film also highlights the importance of journalism and how journalists have the power to uncover conspiracies like the abuse in the Catholic Church or secrets about the Vietnam War as seen in "The Post". However, "Spotlight" isn't the first film to detail the heinous acts committed by members of the Church, films like Francis Ozon's "By the Grace of God" and Pablo Larraín's "The Club" both point out these horrific acts and the impact they had on victims.

Cinematographer Masanobu Takayanagi ("Black Mass", "Stillwater") creates easy on the eye visuals that, despite their monotonous appearance, make this a visually pleasing film. Takaynagi's visuals work with the film's shocking and sensitive story to create one of 2015's best films. Even though "Spotlight" could be considered boring by those who dislike dialogue heavy films, the thought-provoking subject matter keeps your attention for the entire two hours, with audience members wanting to learn details alongside the characters themselves.
